PROP
44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services. Fiscal Impact: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
CON
Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. American Academy of Pediatrics CA, California Medical Association, California Academy of Family Physicians, California School Nurses Organization, doctors, nurses and patients urge NO on 44! www.NOProp44.com

# Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
## Proposition 44: Requires Community Health Clinics to Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
...
### Summary
Proposition 44 began as Initiative 25-0008, filed by Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming in July 2025.
After receiving its official title and summary, the measure was cleared for signature gathering in October 2025.
On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot.
It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services.
No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services.
The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall.

PROP
44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services. Fiscal Impact: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
CON
Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. American Academy of Pediatrics CA, California Medical Association, California Academy of Family Physicians, California School Nurses Organization, doctors, nurses and patients urge NO on 44! www.NOProp44.com

Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Requires Community Health Clinics to Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Spending Requirements for Federally Qualified Health Centers Initiative
Summary
Proposition 44 began as Initiative 25-0008 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming in July 2025. After receiving its official title and summary, the measure was cleared for signature gathering in October 2025. On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot. It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services. The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall. The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years. If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 44 would cost the state in the low tens of millions of dollars each year to enforce the new requirements, including reviewing clinic financial reports and investigating possible violations. These costs would be paid for through fees charged to the clinics as directed by the proposition.
The measure could also affect state and local government spending in other ways, but the costs are uncertain. For example, affected clinics might increase spending on direct patient care to meet the 90% requirement. Because some of those patients are covered by Medi-Cal, this could increase state health care costs. Alternatively, clinics that are unable to meet the requirement could close instead. This could also result in additional costs for state or local governments. The overall fiscal effect is uncertain and would depend largely on how the new spending rules are implemented and how clinics respond to them.
What your vote means
YES: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would be required to use at least 90 percent of their annual revenue to provide health care services.
NO: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would not be subject to the proposed 90 percent spending requirement.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that clinics regularly receive billions of dollars of taxpayer public funds but often spend it in areas not related to patient care. Proposition 44 would ensure more of the public funding received by nonprofit community health clinics goes toward patient care rather than administrative costs and executive compensation. They say the 90% spending requirement would direct more money toward health services while increasing transparency and accountability. Supporters also note that unrecovered penalties would be used to recruit, train, and retain health care workers.
Opponents argue that Proposition 44 is poorly drafted and institutes spending restrictions that could force community health clinics to cut services or close, reducing access to care. They contend that the measure could restrict spending on essential staff, equipment, technology, and other services needed to operate clinics. Opponents also argue that the measure is unnecessary because community health clinics are already subject to state and federal regulations, audits, and oversight.

...
There’s a measure on your California ballot that could change spending rules for community health clinics.
...
Proposition 44 targets federally qualified health centers.
Those are the nonprofit clinics that serve underserved communities across California.
There’s about 2,000 of them.
The ballot measure proposes a new rule: These clinics would have to spend 90% of their revenue on patient care and services tied to their mission.
Right now, they average about 80%.
Miss that target, and the clinic pays a penalty.
They can earn it back if they hit 90% within five years.
If not, the state keeps the money.
Supporters, led by the healthcare union SEIU-UHW, say it stops wasteful spending on executive pay and forces accountability.
Opponents — including both major state parties, Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association — say clinics can’t realistically hit 90%.
One analysis found 89% of California clinic organizations would fail in year one, facing $1.6 billion in fines.

Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Requires Community Health Clinics to Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Spending Requirements for Federally Qualified Health Centers Initiative
Summary
Proposition 44 began as Initiative 25-0008 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming in July 2025. After receiving its official title and summary, the measure was cleared for signature gathering in October 2025. On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot. It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services. The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall. The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years. If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 44 would cost the state in the low tens of millions of dollars each year to enforce the new requirements, including reviewing clinic financial reports and investigating possible violations. These costs would be paid for through fees charged to the clinics as directed by the proposition.
The measure could also affect state and local government spending in other ways, but the costs are uncertain. For example, affected clinics might increase spending on direct patient care to meet the 90% requirement. Because some of those patients are covered by Medi-Cal, this could increase state health care costs. Alternatively, clinics that are unable to meet the requirement could close instead. This could also result in additional costs for state or local governments. The overall fiscal effect is uncertain and would depend largely on how the new spending rules are implemented and how clinics respond to them.
What your vote means
YES: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would be required to use at least 90 percent of their annual revenue to provide health care services.
NO: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would not be subject to the proposed 90 percent spending requirement.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that clinics regularly receive billions of dollars of taxpayer public funds but often spend it in areas not related to patient care. Proposition 44 would ensure more of the public funding received by nonprofit community health clinics goes toward patient care rather than administrative costs and executive compensation. They say the 90% spending requirement would direct more money toward health services while increasing transparency and accountability. Supporters also note that unrecovered penalties would be used to recruit, train, and retain health care workers.
Opponents argue that Proposition 44 is poorly drafted and institutes spending restrictions that could force community health clinics to cut services or close, reducing access to care. They contend that the measure could restrict spending on essential staff, equipment, technology, and other services needed to operate clinics. Opponents also argue that the measure is unnecessary because community health clinics are already subject to state and federal regulations, audits, and oversight.

Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Requires Community Health Clinics to Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Spending Requirements for Federally Qualified Health Centers Initiative
Summary
Proposition 44 began as Initiative 25-0008 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming in July 2025. After receiving its official title and summary, the measure was cleared for signature gathering in October 2025. On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot. It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services. The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall. The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years. If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 44 would cost the state in the low tens of millions of dollars each year to enforce the new requirements, including reviewing clinic financial reports and investigating possible violations. These costs would be paid for through fees charged to the clinics as directed by the proposition.
The measure could also affect state and local government spending in other ways, but the costs are uncertain. For example, affected clinics might increase spending on direct patient care to meet the 90% requirement. Because some of those patients are covered by Medi-Cal, this could increase state health care costs. Alternatively, clinics that are unable to meet the requirement could close instead. This could also result in additional costs for state or local governments. The overall fiscal effect is uncertain and would depend largely on how the new spending rules are implemented and how clinics respond to them.
What your vote means
YES: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would be required to use at least 90 percent of their annual revenue to provide health care services.
NO: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would not be subject to the proposed 90 percent spending requirement.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that clinics regularly receive billions of dollars of taxpayer public funds but often spend it in areas not related to patient care. Proposition 44 would ensure more of the public funding received by nonprofit community health clinics goes toward patient care rather than administrative costs and executive compensation. They say the 90% spending requirement would direct more money toward health services while increasing transparency and accountability. Supporters also note that unrecovered penalties would be used to recruit, train, and retain health care workers.
Opponents argue that Proposition 44 is poorly drafted and institutes spending restrictions that could force community health clinics to cut services or close, reducing access to care. They contend that the measure could restrict spending on essential staff, equipment, technology, and other services needed to operate clinics. Opponents also argue that the measure is unnecessary because community health clinics are already subject to state and federal regulations, audits, and oversight.

PROP
44
Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Summary
Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services. Fiscal Impact: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.

What your vote means
Yes
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
No
A NO vote on this measure means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
More on Proposition 44
For background on Proposition 44, an analysis by the legislative analyst, endorsements for and against the measure, and more...
Read the California Voter Information Guide (http://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/).
Arguments
Pro
Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
Con
Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. American Academy of Pediatrics CA, California Medical Association, California Academy of Family Physicians, California School Nurses Organization, doctors, nurses and patients urge NO on 44! www.NOProp44.com

Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Requires Community Health Clinics to Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Spending Requirements for Federally Qualified Health Centers Initiative
Summary
Proposition 44 began as Initiative 25-0008 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming in July 2025. After receiving its official title and summary, the measure was cleared for signature gathering in October 2025. On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot. It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services. The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall. The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years. If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 44 would cost the state in the low tens of millions of dollars each year to enforce the new requirements, including reviewing clinic financial reports and investigating possible violations. These costs would be paid for through fees charged to the clinics as directed by the proposition.
The measure could also affect state and local government spending in other ways, but the costs are uncertain. For example, affected clinics might increase spending on direct patient care to meet the 90% requirement. Because some of those patients are covered by Medi-Cal, this could increase state health care costs. Alternatively, clinics that are unable to meet the requirement could close instead. This could also result in additional costs for state or local governments. The overall fiscal effect is uncertain and would depend largely on how the new spending rules are implemented and how clinics respond to them.
What your vote means
YES: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would be required to use at least 90 percent of their annual revenue to provide health care services.
NO: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would not be subject to the proposed 90 percent spending requirement.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that clinics regularly receive billions of dollars of taxpayer public funds but often spend it in areas not related to patient care. Proposition 44 would ensure more of the public funding received by nonprofit community health clinics goes toward patient care rather than administrative costs and executive compensation. They say the 90% spending requirement would direct more money toward health services while increasing transparency and accountability. Supporters also note that unrecovered penalties would be used to recruit, train, and retain health care workers.
Opponents argue that Proposition 44 is poorly drafted and institutes spending restrictions that could force community health clinics to cut services or close, reducing access to care. They contend that the measure could restrict spending on essential staff, equipment, technology, and other services needed to operate clinics. Opponents also argue that the measure is unnecessary because community health clinics are already subject to state and federal regulations, audits, and oversight.

# Prop. 44: Californians to vote on 90% spending rule for community health clinics

*Proposition 44 requires certain private nonprofit healthcare clinics to spend at least 90% of their annual total revenue on patient services.
...
There’s a measure on your California ballot that could change spending rules for community health clinics.
...
Proposition 44 targets federally qualified health centers.
Those are the nonprofit clinics that serve underserved communities across California.
There’s about 2,000 of them.
The ballot measure proposes a new rule: These clinics would have to spend 90% of their revenue on patient care and services tied to their mission.
Right now, they average about 80%.
Miss that target, and the clinic pays a penalty.
They can earn it back if they hit 90% within five years.
If not, the state keeps the money.

Proposition 44
Require more clinic spending on patient care
Proposition 44 would require community clinics that serve low-income patients to spend 90% of their annual revenue on patient care. The measure directs the attorney general to publish guidance on what spending qualifies and allows the state to fine clinics that don’t spend the full 90%. The labor union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put it on the ballot after pushing a similar bill last year that failed. Clinics failed to keep the measure off the ballot with a lawsuit earlier this year.

Support

Summary
Support
Supporters, led by the health workers union SEIU-UHW, argue that clinics should spend more on direct patient care and less on executive pay and overhead. With federal cuts under H.R. 1 — which is expected to leave many more uninsured — looming, supporters say it is especially critical for clinics to prioritize patient care now.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure is unnecessary because community clinics are already heavily regulated by the state and federal governments. They say it would cost clinics more than $1.7 billion in noncompliance fees in the first year, ultimately forcing clinics to significantly reduce services or close.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

Proposition 44
Require more clinic spending on patient care
Proposition 44 would require community clinics that serve low-income patients to spend 90% of their annual revenue on patient care. The measure directs the attorney general to publish guidance on what spending qualifies and allows the state to fine clinics that don’t spend the full 90%. The labor union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put it on the ballot after pushing a similar bill last year that failed. Clinics failed to keep the measure off the ballot with a lawsuit earlier this year.

Summary
Support
Supporters, led by the health workers union SEIU-UHW, argue that clinics should spend more on direct patient care and less on executive pay and overhead. With federal cuts under H.R. 1 — which is expected to leave many more uninsured — looming, supporters say it is especially critical for clinics to prioritize patient care now.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure is unnecessary because community clinics are already heavily regulated by the state and federal governments. They say it would cost clinics more than $1.7 billion in noncompliance fees in the first year, ultimately forcing clinics to significantly reduce services or close.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

With federal cuts under H.R. 1 — which is expected to leave many more uninsured — looming, supporters say it is especially critical for clinics to prioritize patient care now.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure is unnecessary because community clinics are already heavily regulated by the state and federal governments. They say it would cost clinics more than $1.7 billion in noncompliance fees in the first year, ultimately forcing clinics to significantly reduce services or close.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

For each election, staff at the IGS Library compile endorsements from key state newspapers, non-profit organizations, political parties, and unions. For the November election, we begin checking websites for endorsements in mid-September and continue checking weekly until Election Day.

NP = Group stated NO POSITION or NEUTRAL
- [dash] = endorsement could not be located
NOTE: a blank box means the source has not yet been checked and verified.

Proposition 44
Require more clinic spending on patient care
Proposition 44 would require community clinics that serve low-income patients to spend 90% of their annual revenue on patient care. The measure directs the attorney general to publish guidance on what spending qualifies and allows the state to fine clinics that don’t spend the full 90%. The labor union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put it on the ballot after pushing a similar bill last year that failed. Clinics failed to keep the measure off the ballot with a lawsuit earlier this year.

Summary
Support
Supporters, led by the health workers union SEIU-UHW, argue that clinics should spend more on direct patient care and less on executive pay and overhead. With federal cuts under H.R. 1 — which is expected to leave many more uninsured — looming, supporters say it is especially critical for clinics to prioritize patient care now.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure is unnecessary because community clinics are already heavily regulated by the state and federal governments. They say it would cost clinics more than $1.7 billion in noncompliance fees in the first year, ultimately forcing clinics to significantly reduce services or close.

These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

November 3, 2026 General Election Ballot Endorsements
For each election, staff at the IGS Library compile endorsements from key state newspapers, non-profit organizations, political parties, and unions. For the November election, we begin checking websites for endorsements in mid-September and continue checking weekly until Election Day.
Table Coding Key
Y = Yes, the group endorses the measure.
N = No, the group does not endorse the measure.
NP = Group stated NO POSITION or NEUTRAL
- [dash] = endorsement could not be located
NOTE: a blank box means the source has not yet been checked and verified.
Endorsements checked and updated as of November 2, 2026.
Newspapers
Many newspapers require a subscription. Whenever possible, we link to a freely available version online. In other cases, we search Access World News, a UCB licensed database, to identify and link to endorsements. A current CalNet ID and password is required to access the articles.

content.thinking:
**Analyzing Voter Sentiment Shifts**

I'm seeing a significant shift in voter sentiment from September to October 2026. The PPIC survey data reveals a substantial drop in "Yes" votes, from 34% to 25%, while "No" votes jumped from 61% to 71%. This change is quite dramatic, and I'm keen to understand the factors driving this.


**Investigating Opposition to Prop 44**

I'm now looking into the opposition campaign for Proposition 44. I've noted a significant discrepancy in campaign finances: $16.9 million in support versus $38.6 million in opposition. Furthermore, every major newspaper and both major political parties, including the California Democratic Party, are against it. Major medical groups also oppose it, which suggests significant public concern.

PROP
44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services. Fiscal Impact: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
CON
Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. American Academy of Pediatrics CA, California Medical Association, California Academy of Family Physicians, California School Nurses Organization, doctors, nurses and patients urge NO on 44! www.NOProp44.com

### Summary
Proposition 44 began as Initiative 25-0008, filed by Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming in July 2025.
After receiving its official title and summary, the measure was cleared for signature gathering in October 2025.
On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot.
It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services.
No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services.
The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall.

Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Requires Community Health Clinics to Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Spending Requirements for Federally Qualified Health Centers Initiative
Summary
Proposition 44 began as Initiative 25-0008 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming in July 2025. After receiving its official title and summary, the measure was cleared for signature gathering in October 2025. On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot. It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services. The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall. The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years. If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 44 would cost the state in the low tens of millions of dollars each year to enforce the new requirements, including reviewing clinic financial reports and investigating possible violations. These costs would be paid for through fees charged to the clinics as directed by the proposition.
The measure could also affect state and local government spending in other ways, but the costs are uncertain. For example, affected clinics might increase spending on direct patient care to meet the 90% requirement. Because some of those patients are covered by Medi-Cal, this could increase state health care costs. Alternatively, clinics that are unable to meet the requirement could close instead. This could also result in additional costs for state or local governments. The overall fiscal effect is uncertain and would depend largely on how the new spending rules are implemented and how clinics respond to them.
What your vote means
YES: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would be required to use at least 90 percent of their annual revenue to provide health care services.
NO: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would not be subject to the proposed 90 percent spending requirement.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that clinics regularly receive billions of dollars of taxpayer public funds but often spend it in areas not related to patient care. Proposition 44 would ensure more of the public funding received by nonprofit community health clinics goes toward patient care rather than administrative costs and executive compensation. They say the 90% spending requirement would direct more money toward health services while increasing transparency and accountability. Supporters also note that unrecovered penalties would be used to recruit, train, and retain health care workers.
Opponents argue that Proposition 44 is poorly drafted and institutes spending restrictions that could force community health clinics to cut services or close, reducing access to care. They contend that the measure could restrict spending on essential staff, equipment, technology, and other services needed to operate clinics. Opponents also argue that the measure is unnecessary because community health clinics are already subject to state and federal regulations, audits, and oversight.

...
There’s a measure on your California ballot that could change spending rules for community health clinics.
...
Proposition 44 targets federally qualified health centers.
Those are the nonprofit clinics that serve underserved communities across California.
There’s about 2,000 of them.
The ballot measure proposes a new rule: These clinics would have to spend 90% of their revenue on patient care and services tied to their mission.
Right now, they average about 80%.
Miss that target, and the clinic pays a penalty.

If not, the state keeps the money.

Proposition 44
Require more clinic spending on patient care
Proposition 44 would require community clinics that serve low-income patients to spend 90% of their annual revenue on patient care. The measure directs the attorney general to publish guidance on what spending qualifies and allows the state to fine clinics that don’t spend the full 90%. The labor union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put it on the ballot after pushing a similar bill last year that failed. Clinics failed to keep the measure off the ballot with a lawsuit earlier this year.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.

Support

Summary
Support
Supporters, led by the health workers union SEIU-UHW, argue that clinics should spend more on direct patient care and less on executive pay and overhead. With federal cuts under H.R. 1 — which is expected to leave many more uninsured — looming, supporters say it is especially critical for clinics to prioritize patient care now.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure is unnecessary because community clinics are already heavily regulated by the state and federal governments. They say it would cost clinics more than $1.7 billion in noncompliance fees in the first year, ultimately forcing clinics to significantly reduce services or close.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

I'm now looking into the opposition campaign for Proposition 44. I've noted a significant discrepancy in campaign finances: $16.9 million in support versus $38.6 million in opposition. Major medical groups also oppose it, which suggests significant public concern.

**Analyzing Proposition 44's Prospects**

It seems the data paints a clear picture. The polling data from PPIC, spanning September and late October of 2026, shows a stark shift towards "No" on Proposition 44. The most recent poll indicates a substantial 71% "No" vote. Furthermore, fundraising efforts appear to be favoring the "No" campaign. The odds seem overwhelmingly stacked against Proposition 44's passage.
